      "source": "en_GB",
      "content": "British general-interest prose is understated. It states a strong claim plainly and lets the claim carry the emphasis, where American register would reach for an intensifier. Irony and litotes are available and are not read as evasion.

Collective nouns take plural agreement when the members are acting and singular when the body is acting as one: *the team are arguing about it*, *the committee has published its report*. Both are correct; what matters is that the choice is consistent within a passage.

The present perfect covers a recent past that still bears on now: *I've just seen the figures*, *have you eaten?* The simple past in those positions reads as American.

*Have got* is ordinary British usage for possession and obligation — *I've got the file*, *you've got to see this* — and is not an informality to be edited out of general prose.

Prepositions differ in a small, fixed set of places: *at the weekend*, *in hospital*, *different from* or *different to*, *write to somebody*, *meet somebody* rather than *meet with*. None of these is a preference; each is the British form.

Spelling is *-ise* or *-ize* by house style — both are correct British English, *-ise* being the majority convention and *-ize* the Oxford one — but a document uses one throughout. The *-yse* group is invariant: *analyse*, *paralyse*, *catalyse*, in Oxford spelling as in any other.

Quotation marks are single as the outer mark in most British house styles, with double inside; some publications invert this. Follow the document's own choice and make it consistent."
    },
    "review": {
      "source": "en_GB",
      "content": "Read for American vocabulary that has drifted in: *gotten*, *math*, *fall* for autumn, *elevator*, *sidewalk*, *movie theater*, *diaper*, *vacation*, *check* for a restaurant bill. A single one is a slip; a scatter of them means the text was drafted in another variety.

Read for mixed formats in one document — dates written both *24 August 2026* and *August 24, 2026*, currency in both *£* and *$*, times in both *2.30pm* and *2:30 p.m.* Format drift is the clearest evidence of assembly from several sources.

Check *-ise* and *-ize* consistency across the whole document, not paragraph by paragraph. Generated British English is frequently American English with some suffixes changed, and the ones that were missed are where it shows.

British institutional and business prose slides into passive nominal style: *It is anticipated that a review will be undertaken*. Give it back its subject and its verb: *We expect to review it*.

Watch for hedges in chains — *somewhat rather more likely*, *it may perhaps be the case that* — where British understatement has stopped being restraint and become evasion. One hedge does work; three cancel each other.

Check that punctuation inside and outside quotation marks follows one convention. British practice places a mark inside the quotation only when it belongs to the quoted matter.

Check title capitalisation is one system throughout. British house styles differ over whether headings take sentence case or title case, and a document that alternates has chosen neither."
    },
    "anti-slop": {
      "source": "en_GB",
      "content": "The reskinning tell. Generated British English is very often American English with a spelling pass over it, so the vocabulary and the format are what give it away rather than the spelling: *colour* and *organisation* in a text that still writes *gotten*, *2:30 p.m.*, and *$*.

*Whilst*, *amongst*, *utilise*, *endeavour*, and *commence* sprinkled through ordinary prose. Each exists; none is the neutral British choice, and their density is a model reaching for something that sounds British rather than something a British writer would write. *While*, *among*, *use*, *try*, and *start* are the words.

Suffix inconsistency inside one text — *organise* in one paragraph and *recognize* in the next — is a generation artefact rather than a style, and it is worth naming as such rather than silently normalising, because it usually means the passage came from somewhere else.

A concentration of punctuation forms that conflict with the document's convention is a generation tell. Refer to Mechanics for the conventions; this scope does not restate them.

The apologetic opening: *It is perhaps worth noting that*, *One might argue that*, *It would be fair to say that*. British hedging turned into an opening formula that says nothing before the sentence starts."
    }
  }
}

=========== base.md
# The base contract

Write with the clarity and factual precision of a well-edited newspaper or quality magazine. Genre, audience, and purpose override that register: a letter, a speech and an advertisement keep their own character. The selected genre governs craft and form; the resolved language governs idiom, syntax and typography. Examples here illustrate meanings, not English phrases to translate.

## Reader and progression

Give the intended reader what they need to understand, judge or do the thing the text is for. Keep a clear focus, introduce unfamiliar concepts before the reasoning needs them, and order material by that reader's needs rather than the writer's discovery process. Relevant technical detail belongs; unexplained jargon and unrelated background do not.

Make the relations between passages real. A transition may explain a connection, but cannot invent one. Keep paragraphs coherent and give supporting material a clear place beside what it supports. The body and its sections remain intelligible without treating a title, standfirst or subheading as their opening sentence.

Open on something specific to the subject. End with what the job calls for: an earned understanding, conclusion, recommendation or next step. Remove introductions and conclusions that add only an announcement or a generic flourish.

## Expression

Use concrete words, useful verbs and a natural, varied cadence. Keep terminology and reference clear; introduce an unfamiliar abbreviation before using it alone. Choose ordinary words where they suffice and established specialist terms where they give this reader precision.

Let tone and rhetorical devices serve the genre and the meaning. A useful analogy, question, image, fragment or humorous turn can clarify or carry a voice; decoration and manufactured drama cannot. An imagined comparison is recognisable as a comparison, never presented as an event or someone's experience. # ABT

*And, But, Therefore*: Randy Olson's structure connecting a situation and what it puts at stake, a genuine complication or question, and the consequence the material supports. It shapes the reasoning or story without prescribing three paragraphs or visible labels.

Each part moves from the general to the specific. The And gives the situation, then what is at stake in it: what it makes possible or puts at risk, as the material states it. The But names the complication briefly, then its causes. The Therefore says what follows or is done, then how, where something is done. The general orients every reader; the specific gives the part its force.

The reader knows why the situation matters before the complication arrives. A text that opens on its problem leaves the reader asking *so what?* Stakes are facts from the material, never a claim that the subject is important. A calm text often shows them through its situation alone: who has to decide what, and what depends on it. Where the material holds no stakes, state the situation plainly and invent none.

The And holds what the complication needs in order to bite and nothing else, and the complication comes early. How much situation that takes depends on what the reader already knows: somebody inside the subject needs little, somebody outside it more.

An arc has one complication. Other problems are ordered under it as its causes, not beside it, since two problems of equal rank competing for one consequence leave the reader unsure which to follow. The consequence answers what the complication raised. Each part of it takes up a cause the text has given, so a list of actions is sound when every action answers one; an action against a problem the text never raised is an addition, not a consequence. For example: a school records room temperatures before deciding whether to change its heating; the readings locate cold periods but do not explain them; the next investigation links readings to room use.

Apply the structure at the level the genre's task needs. Where a genre's own rules compress, withhold or reorder part of the arc, as when a teaser withholds its resolution, web copy puts the useful words first or an opinion states its position early, the genre governs. A standfirst or lead may give the result early, open question included; the order above governs where the body develops the arc, not that early answer.

Nest or revisit an arc when that helps a complex explanation. # The anti-slop catalogue

Prose that a language model produced, or that a human wrote after reading a great deal of it, fails in a small number of recognisable ways. This is the catalogue of those ways: what each one looks like on the page, why it costs the reader something, and the smallest change that removes it. It is a diagnostic document — a Skill reading it beside the base contract meets no target the contract does not already hold, and a Skill reading it alone has the patterns and their repairs and needs nothing else.

The examples are English because this document is, and they are patterns rather than strings. Apply each by what it does in the target language, and do not look for the English words in it. A word, a phrase, a punctuation convention, or a construction that only exists in one language belongs to that language's own anti-slop guidance instead, where a Skill loads it beside this file.

## The test before a pattern is recorded

Each pattern below says what a phrase looks like, and looking like one is not being one. Make the repair in your head before you record anything: where the text then asserts more, less or something else than it did, or a distinction it drew is gone, the pattern is not present and nothing is recorded. A hedge that marks genuine doubt, a repetition that lands, a contrast the reader really would otherwise draw wrongly — each of them fails that test, and each is left exactly as it stands.

The test comes before the finding rather than after it. A pattern written down reaches whoever repairs it as a defect somebody found, and a guard that only makes the repair careful arrives too late to save the phrase.

Repair with the smallest change that removes a pattern the test admits. The writer's vocabulary, their bluntness, their humour, their admitted uncertainty, and their rhythm are what makes a text theirs; a pass that tidies all of it into even prose has replaced one machine voice with another. Leave a strong sentence alone even where it is unusual.

## The seven patterns

The tone of this text you always describe.

- **Promise:** what the brand promises its audience and wants to be known for.
- **Image:** how the reader perceives the brand today, and whether there is trust to build on or distrust to handle.
- **Mandate:** what the brand can speak about with credibility.
- **Tone of voice:** how the brand sounds.
- **Tone in this text:** the brand's tone of voice and the genre's conventions must both be respected. Where they pull in different directions, choose a compromise that sounds natural to both. If they pull the same way, say so.

Here the message is that of this particular text. It may lie close to the promise, but need not. Write the message as a claim in one sentence. The message need not appear in the text. It can be conveyed indirectly, through what the text is about and where it leads the reader. But you need to know what it is, because it decides which conclusion the text should land in. An example: a company selling a tool for video meetings writes an article about remote work. The article lands in the claim that remote teams work better with short daily check-ins than with long weekly meetings. The company's message is that its tool makes the short check-ins easy. That message may never appear in the text.

## 4. Who is the reader?

Describe the typical reader of content in the chosen genre and the chosen channel. What do they already know about the topic? What do they care about? What makes them want to read this kind of content? Is there something that makes the topic particularly pressing for them right now, for example a season, a piece of news, a decision or a new figure? What you write here about why now should also show in the structure.

## 5. What is the text's angle?

The angle is the particular perspective you choose on the topic. Choose only one. The most common mistake is trying to cover the topic from every direction so that the text becomes comprehensive. The result is a text that says a little about a lot and that the reader finds hard to take in. If you see several good angles, make one text of each. You then get more texts out of the same research, and each becomes clearer. Nor does a topic ever run out. Newspapers write about Christmas baking every year. One year it is about the classics, another about biscuits without sugar and a third about baking with children. Choose the angle that lies closest to the reader and that can carry the message. The hook is what makes the text interesting to the reader. It is the tension that makes the reader want to read to the end: the question, the conflict or the surprise the text promises to resolve. The hook carries the angle. In the structure, the hook becomes ABT's But or PAC's premise. The hook is not the same thing as the opening. A text can begin with a scene or a detail that catches attention, but it is the hook that holds the reader. In short texts the two often coincide. - **Call to action and measure:** what the reader is to do is the text's call to action. It can be direct, for example "contact our sales team". - **Interesting:** What makes the reader find the text interesting to read? Most often it is the hook.
- **Valuable:** What value should the text give the reader? What makes the reader feel the text was worth their time? Most often it is the conclusion and what carries it.

- Does the angle lie close to the reader, and does the hook carry the angle?
- Does the structure resolve the hook's tension, and does it fit the length?
- Is the conclusion what the structure actually lands in, does it carry the message, and does it lie within the brand's mandate?
- Does what the reader understands lead to the effect you have described, and does that effect serve the brand's goals?
- Does anything in the structure conflict with what should be left out?

The whole text in one sentence gives the text's main point and how the text reaches it, in the order the reader meets them, with no fixed pattern.
- **Free structure** suits a text where none of the forms works. Begin with an opening that catches the reader and give the main point early. Then take one step at a time, in logical order, and close with an ending that ties the text together and points forward. Sketch the steps in the order they are to be read. The whole text in one sentence gives the text's main point and how the text reaches it, in the order the reader meets them, with no fixed pattern.

Sketch the ending too. It ties back to the hook and shows that it is resolved, and it carries the text's call to action, directly or indirectly.

Where a genre explicitly advises against a technique, as a report does against ABT and a press release against any arc laid over its news-first order, say so with the genre's reason. A genre's ordinary technique of none is not itself advice against an arc.

## 8. What should be left out?

State boundaries, side tracks you deliberately drop, and claims you cannot substantiate. Include also what lies outside the brand's mandate or what the brand for other reasons cannot or will not say. If a boundary has exceptions, write out where the line goes, for example something that may be reported but not argued for. Refer to the brand's writing guidelines if it has any. Many boundaries become visible only once you sketch the structure.

## 9. What should the reader have understood afterwards?

The answer is the text's conclusion. Write it as a claim in one sentence, not as a topic. "Remote work" is a topic. "Remote teams work better with short daily check-ins than with long weekly meetings" is a conclusion. The conclusion is what the structure lands in, that is ABT's Therefore or PAC's Conclusion, summed up in one sentence. With the genre's own form or free structure, the conclusion is the text's main point. If it cannot be summed up in one sentence, the sketch needs sharpening. The conclusion carries the message, either by stating it or by leading the reader to it. It lies within the brand's mandate and gives the reader something worth their time. What the understanding should lead to you answer in the next question.

## 10. What should the reader feel, think or do afterwards?

Describe the change in the reader the brand wants to bring about with the text. The conclusion is about what the reader understands. This question is about what that leads to.

- **Main effect:** choose one main effect and put it so concretely that it can be decided whether it has been reached. The effect can concern what the reader thinks or feels, for example "sees the brand as the obvious expert in the field". It can also concern what the reader does, for example "signs up for the webinar" or "contacts a salesperson".
- **The way there:** if the main effect is reached in several steps, describe what the reader first needs to see, understand or believe.
- **Call to action and measure:** what the reader is to do is the text's call to action. It can be direct, for example "contact our sales team". It can also be indirect: the text does not say it, but the reader is left with the feeling that they should act and knows how. If the effect can be measured, state also what shows it has been reached, for example sign-ups, clicks or enquiries. If the text deliberately has no call to action or no measure, say so, so that it shows as a choice and not a gap.

## 11. What makes the text RIV for the reader, and does the brief hold together?

This question checks that everything above serves the reader and holds together. Answer from what you have already written and state where in the structure each part is found. If something is missing there, add it now.

- **Relevant:** What makes the text relevant to the reader and their situation? Why should they read it at all? Is what makes the topic pressing right now part of the structure? The text must at least be relevant.
- **Interesting:** What makes the reader find the text interesting to read? Most often it is the hook.
- **Valuable:** What value should the text give the reader? What makes the reader feel the text was worth their time? Most often it is the conclusion and what carries it.

Then read the answers in one sweep and check that the chain holds:

- Does the reader follow from the sender and the channel?
- Does the angle lie close to the reader, and does the hook carry the angle?
- Does the structure resolve the hook's tension, and does it fit the length?
- Is the conclusion what the structure actually lands in, does it carry the message, and does it lie within the brand's mandate?
- Does what the reader understands lead to the effect you have described, and does that effect serve the brand's goals?
- Does anything in the structure conflict with what should be left out?

Write the check down: answer yes, no or partly to each question and give a short reason. Fix what does not hold together now. It is much easier than fixing it in a finished draft. Questions about the direction, that is the angle, the message and the conclusion, need to be settled before you write. Questions that need more research you write down as open questions and settle during the work.

## 12. What sources do you know of, and what do you need to find out?

A brief is often written before the research is done, and the research is often part of the assignment. Write down the sources you already know of or know you have access to, for example reports, statistics, earlier texts and interviews. Link also to the brand's platform or tone-of-voice guide, if you have not already done so under the sender. Link where you can and number the sources. If you already know that a claim in the sketch can be substantiated, refer to the source there. Add to the list as you find more, and note what you need to find out. It is no requirement that everything in the brief is substantiated. The requirement applies to the finished text. There every claim must be possible to substantiate with a source, an interview or your research, or be a generally accepted claim that the sender can make without risk.

A brief-shortfall finding also carries its numbered requirement and exact, attributed supporting passages supplied by the parent review. Those are part of the finding, not an extra interpretation.

Tell the subagent nothing else. Not what an earlier round found, not what an earlier correction attempted, not which findings you think matter most, and not your reading of what the text is trying to do — that reading is the thing a fresh subagent is dispatched to be without.

Never write it to a file and send a path in its place: this brief holds the user's text entire and every finding standing against it, and a file is a name some other process can read, replace, or delete for as long as the round lasts. A long text makes a long brief, and a long brief is passed whole anyway — trimming it, summarising it, and pointing at it are the three things this brief exists to rule out.

---

You are making one correction to one text. You have not seen this text before, and there is nothing you are expected to remember: the text below is its current state, and the findings below are the current review's, complete and as they were written. Repair them.

**The text.** This is the complete Text Artifact, exactly as it now stands:

`<text>`

**The findings.** This is every finding the review recorded against that text, complete and in the order it recorded them:

`<findings>`

**The contract.** The text is a `<genre>` in `<language>`, and it is held to `<technique>`. Read what it is held to before you change anything: `<library>/references/editorial/base.md` and `<library>/references/editorial/base.review.md`; `<library>/references/editorial/genres/<genre>.md` and the `.review.md` file beside it where one exists; `<library>/references/editorial/techniques/<technique>.md` and its `.review.md` the same way; `<library>/references/editorial/anti-slop.md`; and the `composition`, `review` and `anti-slop` scopes of the resolved language, which `uv run "<library>/scripts/languages.py" resolve --scope=composition --scope=review --scope=anti-slop "<language>"` returns. For `article`, `casestudy`, `column` and `opinion`, and for `webcopy`, also read `<library>/references/editorial/web-craft.md` and `<library>/references/editorial/web-craft.review.md`; for `article`, `casestudy`, `column` and `opinion` alone, also read `<library>/references/editorial/article-anatomy.md` and `<library>/references/editorial/article-anatomy.review.md`, which fix the parts, order and dimensions of such a text; and for those four and for `pressrelease`, also read `<library>/references/editorial/headlines.md` and `<library>/references/editorial/headlines.review.md`, which say how a headline and its subheadings are written. These are the only additional genre support files: follow no other genre links and load no unselected genre or technique. A review extension that is not there is not a defect. Run the resolver with `UV_NO_CACHE=1 UV_NO_PROJECT=1` and a fresh private `TMPDIR`, removing that directory afterwards, including on failure. Load no mechanics guidance and correct no spelling, punctuation, or grammar: a mechanical pass runs after you, and work you do there is work done twice.

**What you change, and what you preserve.** Repair what the findings name and nothing else. Every difference between the text you return and the text above is traced to a finding, or to what repairing a finding required, before this round is accepted, and a difference that traces to no finding is restored from the text you received — so a phrase you improved outside a finding is work that will be undone. Preserve everything the findings do not concern: every sentence, every fact, every quotation, every code sample, every heading, every piece of formatting and every line of frontmatter among them comes back exactly as you received it — a repair that improves a paragraph nobody complained about is a change nobody asked for and nobody will review. A code sample — a fenced block, an indented block, or an inline code span — is quoted material rather than the text's own prose: its contents are read past rather than read against the rules, so nothing inside one is a finding and nothing inside one is changed, the docstrings, comments, and string literals among them. Prose about code is ordinary prose and is read like every other sentence. Where a finding can be repaired several ways, make the smallest change that removes it. Where a finding names something you cannot repair without inventing a fact, changing what the text claims, or altering a quotation's meaning, stance, certainty or distinctive wording, leave that passage alone and say so: in an ordinary review this text is answerable to material you do not have, and a plausible invention is worse than an unrepaired finding. For a brief-shortfall finding carrying exact source support, use only that support or the text to supply what is missing. A repair never states the sender's message outright, since the message may always be conveyed indirectly. Source Fidelity binds the repair: retain attribution, uncertainty, scope, chronology, causality and quotation meaning. A requirement in the brief is not source evidence; where the finding has no support for a needed fact, source or quotation, leave it for the writer and report why.

**A defect of your own costs the whole round.** The review that follows you establishes whether this text has a defect it did not have when you received it — a headline or a heading claiming more than the text claims, a heading repeating the passage under it, a limit your repair dropped. Where it establishes one, the whole round is rejected: the text you received is restored entire, nothing you did survives however much else you repaired, and no fresh attempt follows. So a finding you cannot repair without creating another one is a finding you leave and say so, exactly as you would one you cannot repair without inventing a fact — an unrepaired finding a person can settle costs less than a repair that has to be thrown away with everything beside it.

**What a repair may take with it, and what it may not.** A finding names a defect, and what a repair removes is that defect. Where the defect a finding names is the whole of the passage — an opening that would sit in front of any text, a closing that restates what the reader has just read, a claim credited to nobody that the text cannot source — removing it may be the repair, and any claim removed with it must be named in your return. That stops at a sentence whose work is to bound what the text asserts — that something is not measured, not claimed, not witnessed or not general, or that the text is an observation of a document rather than a scene from an occasion. Remove or weaken one only where the finding names a defect inside the sentence, and only where a sentence you keep still states that limit in full, so the text bounds what it claims exactly as far as it did, or where the limit contradicts another passage of the same text. Otherwise leave it exactly as it stands and say so. Where the passage carries a claim beside the defect — a fact, an observation, the point the passage exists to make — the smallest change is the one that leaves that claim standing, and deleting the passage entire is not that change. And where you can see no way to remove the defect that does not take the claim with it, leave the passage alone and say so, exactly as you would a finding you cannot repair without inventing a fact: a person can give that claim what it needs or let it go, and a round that deletes it leaves them nothing to weigh. That judgement is about the passage in front of you and never about how much of the text is left — a short text is no licence to leave a finding standing, and a long one is no licence to go on cutting.

A repair at a punctuation joint can be the smallest change even when the finding names the implication created there rather than punctuation itself. In *We finished in March, the finance team got a new reporting tool the same month.*, the defect is the implication created by joining unrelated claims, not either claim. Repair it as *We finished in March. The finance team got a new reporting tool the same month.*: splitting at the joint removes the implication and keeps the reporting-tool fact. Do the same wherever the named defect is confined to a joint; do not delete either side or supply a relationship the text does not establish. This example does not admit a wider mechanics pass: it identifies the smallest repair for the finding already in hand.

Before you return the text, compare it before and after, claim by claim. Every claim you received must still appear with its scope, certainty, attribution, chronology, causality and meaning intact unless the finding named the whole claim as the defect; that exception does not reach a sentence whose work is to bound what the text asserts, which goes only on the two conditions above, and the number or concentration of findings changes nothing about that check. The concentrated anti-slop case makes the boundary visible: removing its patterns must not discard its claims about meeting load, documentation, decisions, satisfaction, distributed work, adoption conditions, or the synchronous/asynchronous trade-off. Repair the patterns around those claims. If one cannot be separated from its pattern, keep it and report the finding unresolved; never compress several content-bearing passages into a cleaner summary.

Where the text is an `article`, a `casestudy`, a `column` or an `opinion`, measure it before you return it: run `uv run "<library>/scripts/article_anatomy.py" -` with the complete corrected text on stdin, under the same `UV_NO_CACHE=1 UV_NO_PROJECT=1` and fresh private `TMPDIR` terms as the resolver above. Exit 0 settles the counted requirements only: it says they hold and nothing about the anatomy requirements the script does not count, so your return reports the text as conforming to the anatomy only where you examined every one of those too, and otherwise names the ones you did not examine. Exit 1 names each counted requirement of the article anatomy that fails, with the part, the rule and the figure measured: repair the ones a finding named and the ones your own repair introduced, then measure again, except a part a finding names as absent and a failure caused only by an absent part, which you leave unwritten and name in your return as left for a person to supply; a requirement the text was already failing when it reached you, and that no finding names, is left exactly as it stands like everything else the findings do not concern. Exit 2 says the script could not measure the text, and your return says so. Read every `heading_pairs` entry against the complete candidate and the loaded headline contract before returning, whatever the exit status: judge whether each part adds different information in different wording. Necessary repeated names and topic words can be legitimate, and a paraphrased echo can share no words; `shared_words` alone never authorizes a change or creates a finding. Verify absent or ambiguous sentence estimates against the text; on exit 2 inspect the pairs by hand. Repair echoes named by the findings or introduced by your own correction by wording the heading from its whole text or section without strengthening its claims and without pre-spending the judgement, figure or concession of a quotation standing under a subheading, then measure again. An unrelated pre-existing echo stays as received and is reported in your return, with the pair and reader loss; the evidence does not expand your correction authority. Report any echo you cannot repair within that authority the same way.

Where the text is a `pressrelease`, measure it before you return it the same way, with `--genre=pressrelease` before the `-`, which measures the two counted limits the genre states and nothing else of it. Exit 1 names the headline or the summary that is past its limit, with the rule and the figure measured: repair the ones a finding named and the ones your own repair introduced, then measure again, except a summary a finding names as absent, which you leave unwritten and name in your return as left for a person to supply; a limit the text was already failing when it reached you, and that no finding names, is left exactly as it stands. Exit 2 says the script found no level-1 heading or could not read the text, and your return says so. The output carries no heading pairs: read the headline and the summary against each other as the genre's review half says before returning.

**Your own working files.** Any file you write for your own working purposes — a candidate you measure, a draft you compare, anything you keep while you work — goes in a directory you created for this one round, under a name made unique when you created it, such as the one `mktemp -d` returns. Remove that directory before you return, including on failure. A fixed name under a shared temporary directory is not that directory, whether the directory is the system's own or a scratchpad your session was given: another run may be working at the same time, in the same place and on this same text, and write that same name. The file you come back to is then that run's work and not yours, and when you take it for your own stale copy and delete or replace it, you destroy work that is not yours, and nothing tells the run it came from.

**What you return.** The complete corrected text and a short note of which findings you repaired and which you left, with the reason for each you left. Where any repair removed a passage carrying a claim, name every removed claim and say which finding made the claim itself the defect, and name every changed claim the same way — one you left standing with its scope, certainty, attribution, chronology, causality or meaning moved, by what it now asserts rather than how far its wording moved, and the finding the repair that moved it answered. Where a repair took a limit, a connective or a bounding clause out of the text — a sentence or a heading saying what is not measured, not claimed or not known, a connective giving the text's own reason for what follows, a clause saying what a claim is not about — say what a reader of the text you return no longer has, however little of the text went with it. Name every added claim the same way, whether or not anything was removed: one the text you return asserts and the text you received has no counterpart for, an inference drawn from what that text already said among them where it asserts something that text did not say, and the finding the repair that wrote it answered. A claim with a counterpart in the text you received is changed rather than added. Reporting a removal never makes an impermissible one acceptable. The complete text: not a diff, not the changed passages, not a description of what you did. Return no commentary inside the text itself.
======
# The reply check

Give this to a subagent started fresh once step 9 has produced the final Text Artifact and the reply is drafted, before anything is delivered. It runs on every run whose reply says anything about a text, which is every run except one that returns only the short no-change status. Everything in angle brackets is replaced; nothing else is rewritten.

`<received>` is the Text Artifact as it arrived, pasted whole, frontmatter included. `<delivered>` is the final Text Artifact step 9 produced, pasted whole. `<reply>` is the reply as drafted, pasted whole: every finding, the claim account, the closing paragraph and every other sentence it will deliver, leaving out only the delivered text where the reply carries it. `<measurement>` is, for `article`, `casestudy`, `column`, `opinion` and `pressrelease`, the full output of step 6's command run on the delivered text, as step 11 says, pasted whole; for any other genre, drop the paragraph headed **The measurement of the delivered text** and the placeholder under it. `<library>` is the Collection Library path this run resolved.

Tell the subagent nothing else. Not the review's reasoning, not the rounds or what any of them attempted, not why any change was made, and not this Skill's own instructions: the checker is a reader who knows what the reader of the reply will know, the two texts and what the reply says of them, and that is what lets it see what a change did beyond what it was meant to do. Hand the filled-in brief to the subagent directly, as the whole of its instruction, and never as a file whose path you send in its place: it holds the user's text twice, and a file is a name another process can read, replace or delete while the check runs.

**What you do with what it returns.** The subagent returns two lists. Act on every item of both, and correct only the reply:

- A statement on the first list is rewritten so that it is true of the text it names, or left out, as *The truth of a report about the text* in `$LIBRARY/references/delivery.md` says. A count or length about the delivered text takes its figure from the measurement you handed over.
- A difference on the second list is added to the claim account, or its entry completed, the way step 11 reports a removed, changed or added claim. Anything the reply says about the claims as a whole that the new or completed entry contradicts is narrowed to what holds, or left out.

The list is a check of the reply, not a note of what a correction did, so the closing paragraph is still built from your own comparison of the two texts, and is corrected from the list like every other statement. The text is not touched: the Text Artifact step 9 produced is delivered as it is, and step 10 holds. The check is made once, and the corrected reply is delivered without being checked again.

---

You are checking one reply against the two texts it describes. You did not write the reply and you did not make the changes it reports; you know only what is below, which is what the reply's own reader will know. Find what the reply gets wrong about the texts, and only that: whether a change was a good one, whether a finding was worth making and how the text reads are questions for somebody else.

**The text as it arrived.** This is the complete text the run received:

`<received>`

**The text as delivered.** This is the complete text the run delivers:

`<delivered>`

**The reply.** This is everything the run is about to say about the two texts:

`<reply>`

**The measurement of the delivered text.** This is the full output of the collection's measuring script, run on the delivered text. A count or length the reply states about the delivered text is read against it:

`<measurement>`

**The duties the reply is held to.** Before you read the reply, read two passages and apply them as written: the section *The truth of a report about the text* in `<library>/references/delivery.md`, and the sentences of `<library>/references/editorial/base.review.md` that say what the claim account holds, from *A claim removed because the finding named that claim itself* to the end of that paragraph. Read nothing else of either file, and no other file.

**First compare the two texts yourself**, passage by passage, frontmatter and headings included, and note every difference, before you read what the reply says about them. The reply's own account is what you are checking, so it is never how you find a difference.

**Then return two lists.**

1. **False statements.** Every statement of the reply that the text it names contradicts, read as *The truth of a report about the text* reads it: a statement about the text as it arrived against that text, and every other statement against the delivered text. A finding's description of a passage, a count, a length, a grammatical label, where a passage stands, what a round did to a passage, a statement that something holds everywhere or nowhere, and every entry and sentence of the claim account are statements the text can contradict. A judgement of quality — that a heading was vague, that a passage read as filler — is not. For each: quote the statement, name the text it is about, quote the passage that contradicts it, and say what is true.
2. **Claim changes the account misses.** Every difference between the two texts that moves a claim and that the claim account leaves out, or reports short of what it did: scope narrowed or widened; a condition, a qualification, a limit or a connective lost; chronology, causality or attribution moved; or the meaning moved, a sense or a double sense lost and an actor, an ordering or a framing added among it. A headline, a standfirst and a subheading carry claims like any other passage. For each: quote the passage before and after, say what the difference did to the claim, and quote what the account says of it, or say that it says nothing.

Write `none` under a list with nothing on it. Return the two lists and nothing else, and write no file.

A repair never states the sender's message outright, since the message may always be conveyed indirectly. Source Fidelity binds the repair: retain attribution, uncertainty, scope, chronology, causality and quotation meaning. A requirement in the brief is not source evidence; where the finding has no support for a needed fact, source or quotation, leave it for the writer and report why.

**A defect of your own costs the whole round.** The review that follows you establishes whether this text has a defect it did not have when you received it — a headline or a heading claiming more than the text claims, a heading repeating the passage under it, a limit your repair dropped. Where it establishes one, the whole round is rejected: the text you received is restored entire, nothing you did survives however much else you repaired, and no fresh attempt follows. So a finding you cannot repair without creating another one is a finding you leave and say so, exactly as you would one you cannot repair without inventing a fact — an unrepaired finding a person can settle costs less than a repair that has to be thrown away with everything beside it.

**What a repair may take with it, and what it may not.** A finding names a defect, and what a repair removes is that defect. Where the defect a finding names is the whole of the passage — an opening that would sit in front of any text, a closing that restates what the reader has just read, a claim credited to nobody that the text cannot source — removing it may be the repair, and any claim removed with it must be named in your return. That stops at a sentence whose work is to bound what the text asserts — that something is not measured, not claimed, not witnessed or not general, or that the text is an observation of a document rather than a scene from an occasion. Remove or weaken one only where the finding names a defect inside the sentence, and only where a sentence you keep still states that limit in full, so the text bounds what it claims exactly as far as it did, or where the limit contradicts another passage of the same text. Otherwise leave it exactly as it stands and say so. Where the passage carries a claim beside the defect — a fact, an observation, the point the passage exists to make — the smallest change is the one that leaves that claim standing, and deleting the passage entire is not that change. And where you can see no way to remove the defect that does not take the claim with it, leave the passage alone and say so, exactly as you would a finding you cannot repair without inventing a fact: a person can give that claim what it needs or let it go, and a round that deletes it leaves them nothing to weigh. That judgement is about the passage in front of you and never about how much of the text is left — a short text is no licence to leave a finding standing, and a long one is no licence to go on cutting.

A repair at a punctuation joint can be the smallest change even when the finding names the implication created there rather than punctuation itself. In *We finished in March, the finance team got a new reporting tool the same month.*, the defect is the implication created by joining unrelated claims, not either claim. Repair it as *We finished in March. The finance team got a new reporting tool the same month.*: splitting at the joint removes the implication and keeps the reporting-tool fact. Do the same wherever the named defect is confined to a joint; do not delete either side or supply a relationship the text does not establish. This example does not admit a wider mechanics pass: it identifies the smallest repair for the finding already in hand.

Before you return the text, compare it before and after, claim by claim. Every claim you received must still appear with its scope, certainty, attribution, chronology, causality and meaning intact unless the finding named the whole claim as the defect; that exception does not reach a sentence whose work is to bound what the text asserts, which goes only on the two conditions above, and the number or concentration of findings changes nothing about that check. The concentrated anti-slop case makes the boundary visible: removing its patterns must not discard its claims about meeting load, documentation, decisions, satisfaction, distributed work, adoption conditions, or the synchronous/asynchronous trade-off. Repair the patterns around those claims. If one cannot be separated from its pattern, keep it and report the finding unresolved; never compress several content-bearing passages into a cleaner summary.

Where the text is an `article`, a `casestudy`, a `column` or an `opinion`, measure it before you return it: run `uv run "<library>/scripts/article_anatomy.py" -` with the complete corrected text on stdin, under the same `UV_NO_CACHE=1 UV_NO_PROJECT=1` and fresh private `TMPDIR` terms as the resolver above. Exit 0 settles the counted requirements only: it says they hold and nothing about the anatomy requirements the script does not count, so your return reports the text as conforming to the anatomy only where you examined every one of those too, and otherwise names the ones you did not examine. Exit 1 names each counted requirement of the article anatomy that fails, with the part, the rule and the figure measured: repair the ones a finding named and the ones your own repair introduced, then measure again, except a part a finding names as absent and a failure caused only by an absent part, which you leave unwritten and name in your return as left for a person to supply; a requirement the text was already failing when it reached you, and that no finding names, is left exactly as it stands like everything else the findings do not concern. Exit 2 says the script could not measure the text, and your return says so. Read every `heading_pairs` entry against the complete candidate and the loaded headline contract before returning, whatever the exit status: judge whether each part adds different information in different wording. Necessary repeated names and topic words can be legitimate, and a paraphrased echo can share no words; `shared_words` alone never authorizes a change or creates a finding. Verify absent or ambiguous sentence estimates against the text; on exit 2 inspect the pairs by hand. Repair echoes named by the findings or introduced by your own correction by wording the heading from its whole text or section without strengthening its claims and without pre-spending the judgement, figure or concession of a quotation standing under a subheading, then measure again. An unrelated pre-existing echo stays as received and is reported in your return, with the pair and reader loss; the evidence does not expand your correction authority. Report any echo you cannot repair within that authority the same way.

Where the text is a `pressrelease`, measure it before you return it the same way, with `--genre=pressrelease` before the `-`, which measures the two counted limits the genre states and nothing else of it. Exit 1 names the headline or the summary that is past its limit, with the rule and the figure measured: repair the ones a finding named and the ones your own repair introduced, then measure again, except a summary a finding names as absent, which you leave unwritten and name in your return as left for a person to supply; a limit the text was already failing when it reached you, and that no finding names, is left exactly as it stands. A fixed name under a shared temporary directory is not that directory, whether the directory is the system's own or a scratchpad your session was given: another run may be working at the same time, in the same place and on this same text, and write that same name. The file you come back to is then that run's work and not yours, and when you take it for your own stale copy and delete or replace it, you destroy work that is not yours, and nothing tells the run it came from.

**What you return.** The complete corrected text and a short note of which findings you repaired and which you left, with the reason for each you left. Name every added claim the same way, whether or not anything was removed: one the text you return asserts and the text you received has no counterpart for, an inference drawn from what that text already said among them where it asserts something that text did not say, and the finding the repair that wrote it answered. Everything in angle brackets is replaced; nothing else is rewritten.

The list is a check of the reply, not a note of what a correction did, so the closing paragraph is still built from your own comparison of the two texts, and is corrected from the list like every other statement. The text is not touched: the Text Artifact step 9 produced is delivered as it is, and step 10 holds. The check is made once, and the corrected reply is delivered without being checked again.

You are checking one reply against the two texts it describes. You did not write the reply and you did not make the changes it reports; you know only what is below, which is what the reply's own reader will know. **The text as it arrived.** This is the complete text the run received:

`<received>`

**The text as delivered.** This is the complete text the run delivers:

`<delivered>`

**The reply.** This is everything the run is about to say about the two texts:

`<reply>`

**The measurement of the delivered text.** This is the full output of the collection's measuring script, run on the delivered text. A count or length the reply states about the delivered text is read against it:

**The duties the reply is held to.** Before you read the reply, read two passages and apply them as written: the section *The truth of a report about the text* in `<library>/references/delivery.md`, and the sentences of `<library>/references/editorial/base.review.md` that say what the claim account holds, from *A claim removed because the finding named that claim itself* to the end of that paragraph. **First compare the two texts yourself**, passage by passage, frontmatter and headings included, and note every difference, before you read what the reply says about them. The reply's own account is what you are checking, so it is never how you find a difference.

**Then return two lists.**

1. **False statements.** Every statement of the reply that the text it names contradicts, read as *The truth of a report about the text* reads it: a statement about the text as it arrived against that text, and every other statement against the delivered text. A finding's description of a passage, a count, a length, a grammatical label, where a passage stands, what a round did to a passage, a statement that something holds everywhere or nowhere, and every entry and sentence of the claim account are statements the text can contradict. A judgement of quality — that a heading was vague, that a passage read as filler — is not. For each: quote the statement, name the text it is about, quote the passage that contradicts it, and say what is true.
2. **Claim changes the account misses.** Every difference between the two texts that moves a claim and that the claim account leaves out, or reports short of what it did: scope narrowed or widened; a condition, a qualification, a limit or a connective lost; chronology, causality or attribution moved; or the meaning moved, a sense or a double sense lost and an actor, an ordering or a framing added among it. # Ten minutes on a Friday

For four years, Priya Nand kept her receipts in a biscuit tin. She tutors maths in Leeds, and every January the tin came down from the shelf. "The last weekend of January was always gone," she says. The Self Assessment return is due on 31 January, and most of us spend the months before it the way Priya did, with receipts collecting in a drawer or an inbox until there is no more room for later.

The tin has two costs. The first is the weekend. The second is quieter. Till receipts are printed on thermal paper, and they often fade within months, faster in a warm kitchen. When Priya finally opened the tin one January, two receipts from the spring had faded to blank, and she could not claim them.

The usual advice is a weekly habit: photograph each receipt, match the week's photographs to your bank lines every Friday, and note anything odd. It is good advice, and it asks for fifty-two Fridays a year from people who already work most of them.

There is another way to get the weekend back. In a survey this summer, 412 of our users told us how long their last return took. Those who matched receipts every week reported a median of 6 hours of their own time. Those who left everything until January reported 19. But the 57 whose return was prepared by an accountant reported a median of just 3 hours. The figures are what people told us rather than anything we measured, and they do not show what caused the difference. Still, the shortest January in the survey belonged to the people who did the least bookkeeping themselves.

A tutor's time is worth more at the whiteboard than at the kitchen table sorting paper. The tin does not have to become a Friday chore. It can become somebody else's job.

This January, the tin could leave the house before the last weekend does.
````

But the 57 whose return was prepared by an accountant reported a median of just 3 hours. The figures are what people told us rather than anything we measured, and they do not show what caused the difference. Still, the shortest January in the survey belonged to the people who did the least bookkeeping themselves.

I repaired findings 1 to 5 and left findings 6 and 7 for the writer. The genre is `general`, so no measuring script applied. The only temporary directory was the resolver's private `TMPDIR`, and it has been removed.

````markdown
# Ten minutes on a Friday

For four years, Priya Nand kept her receipts in a biscuit tin. She tutors maths in Leeds, and every January the tin came down from the shelf. "The last weekend of January was always gone," she says. The Self Assessment return is due on 31 January, and most of us spend the months before it the way Priya did, with receipts collecting in a drawer or an inbox until there is no more room for later.

The tin has two costs. The first is the weekend. The second is quieter. Till receipts are printed on thermal paper, and they often fade within months, faster in a warm kitchen. When Priya finally opened the tin one January, two receipts from the spring had faded to blank, and she could not claim them.

The usual advice is a weekly habit: photograph each receipt, match the week's photographs to your bank lines every Friday, and note anything odd. In March 2026, Priya moved to a session every Friday. "About ten minutes, with a cup of tea," she says.

In a survey this summer, 412 of our users told us how long their last return took. Those who matched receipts every week reported a median of 6 hours of their own time. Those who left everything until January reported 19. But the 57 whose return was prepared by an accountant reported a median of just 3 hours. The figures are what people told us rather than anything we measured, and they do not show what caused the difference.

Priya photographs each receipt when she gets it, and a photograph taken while the receipt is new stays readable.

The next receipt you get can be photographed there and then, and matched this Friday.
````

**Repaired**
- **Finding 1:** I removed the sentences that dismiss the weekly habit and turn to an accountant, and replaced the ending with the weekly habit. I kept all the survey figures, including the accountant figure and the "But ... just" sentence, which the finding calls supported. The sentence saying the figures don't show cause is unchanged.
- **Finding 2:** The new paragraph 5 answers the second cost, the faded receipts, using material.md §2 and §3.
- **Finding 3:** Paragraph 3 now gives Priya's move to a Friday session and how long it takes (material.md §2).
- **Finding 4:** The body now carries the ten-minute Friday session, so the title stays as it is, as the finding's note allows.
- **Finding 5:** The unsupported sentence is gone (see removed claims below).

**Left for the writer**
- **Finding 6:** "most of us spend the months before it the way Priya did" and "The usual advice is a weekly habit" are unchanged. The material doesn't support either claim, and the finding says not to repair it.
- **Finding 7:** Nothing is added about the early-October send-out or the time left before January. The material has nothing on it.

**Removed claims**
- "It is good advice" and "it asks for fifty-two Fridays a year from people who already work most of them" (Findings 1 and 3).
- "There is another way to get the weekend back" (Finding 1).
- "the shortest January in the survey belonged to the people who did the least bookkeeping themselves" (Findings 1 and 5).
- "A tutor's time is worth more at the whiteboard than at the kitchen table sorting paper" (Finding 1).
- "The tin does not have to become a Friday chore. It can become somebody else's job." (Finding 1).
- "This January, the tin could leave the house before the last weekend does." (Finding 1).
- **Connective removed:** "Still," is gone with the Finding 5 sentence. Readers lose the text's conclusion, drawn despite the survey's limits, that least bookkeeping went with the shortest January. The sentence limiting the figures is still there in full.

**Added claims**
- In March 2026, Priya moved to a session every Friday, and she describes it as "About ten minutes, with a cup of tea" (Finding 3, from material.md §2).
- Priya photographs each receipt when she gets it (Finding 2, from material.md §2).
- A photograph taken while the receipt is new stays readable (Finding 2, from material.md §3).
- The new closing line is a next step with no new fact: the next receipt can be photographed when you get it and matched this Friday (Finding 1). It uses the steps the text already gives. It doesn't say the habit shortens January, so the survey's no-cause limit still holds.

No claim was changed.

# Ten minutes on a Friday

For four years, Priya Nand kept her receipts in a biscuit tin. She tutors maths in Leeds, and every January the tin came down from the shelf. "The last weekend of January was always gone," she says. The Self Assessment return is due on 31 January, and most of us spend the months before it the way Priya did, with receipts collecting in a drawer or an inbox until there is no more room for later.

The tin has two costs. The first is the weekend. The second is quieter. Till receipts are printed on thermal paper, and they often fade within months, faster in a warm kitchen. When Priya finally opened the tin one January, two receipts from the spring had faded to blank, and she could not claim them.

The usual advice is a weekly habit: photograph each receipt, match the week's photographs to your bank lines every Friday, and note anything odd. In March 2026, Priya moved to a session every Friday. "About ten minutes, with a cup of tea," she says.

In a survey this summer, 412 of our users told us how long their last return took. Those who matched receipts every week reported a median of 6 hours of their own time. Those who left everything until January reported 19. But the 57 whose return was prepared by an accountant reported a median of just 3 hours. The figures are what people told us rather than anything we measured, and they do not show what caused the difference.

Priya photographs each receipt when she gets it, and a photograph taken while the receipt is new stays readable.

The next receipt you get can be photographed there and then, and matched this Friday.
EOF

# The mechanics contract

Objective correctness, in the half of it that does not depend on which language a text is in. A Skill contracted to mechanical correction reads this document together with the resolved language's own mechanics guidance, and the two together are that run's rules. What is true of every language the Collection installs is stated here and stated once, so that it is not written again in each language, where the copies would be free to disagree with one another about what is an error.

Nothing here is a preference. A rule belongs in this document only where the text is wrong whatever the writer intended, and only where it would be wrong in the same way in any language. Spelling, inflection, agreement, the language's own punctuation, and its conventions for dates, numbers, currency, and quotation all turn on the language and belong to that language's resource. Where a language defaults more strictly or more loosely than a rule below, its own guidance says so, and what it says about itself wins.

The examples are English because this document is, and they are patterns rather than strings. Apply each by what it does in the target language rather than by the words it happens to use.

## Clause boundaries

Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone are an error where the second does not explain, specify, restate, or stand in direct contrast to the first. *The project will be expensive, it starts in the spring* puts two statements in one sentence that have nothing to do with each other beyond sitting there together: the reader takes the comma as a signal that the sentence continues, and meets a new subject and a new verb instead. Two clauses run together with no punctuation at the joint at all are the same error, and take the same correction.

The same joint is not an error where the second clause does explain, specify, restate, or contrast with the first. *The bug was not in the parser, it was in a silent retry* is the negative-positive contrast, where the comma is what holds the two halves together as one statement, and separating them would break a single thought into two. *We shipped it anyway, nobody had a better idea* specifies the first clause with the reason behind it. Both are established usage rather than tolerated looseness, and a pass that corrects them has changed how the sentence reads without being asked to.

Judge a joint by whether the clauses cohere, and not by their length, by how formal the text is, or by how the text punctuates elsewhere. Where the reading is genuinely open — where a careful reader could defend the joint — the comma stands, because what this rule reaches is the boundary that misleads and not the boundary that is merely informal.

Correct an erroneous joint at the joint and nowhere else: the comma becomes a period or a semicolon, and nothing else about the sentence moves. Do not reorder the clauses, do not merge them into one, and do not supply a conjunction — *and*, *but*, and *so* each assert a relation between the two clauses, and the writer asserted none. Neither half is rewritten, split, or tightened on the way past. Where more than one of a period and a semicolon would serve, the period is the safer of the two, since it claims nothing about how closely the statements are related.

## Quotation

Quoted matter reaches a reader in one of three settings, and the setting decides what the punctuation and capitalisation around it have to do. A quotation is run into a sentence, set off as a block of its own, or reported as speech, and a reader takes each of the three as a different promise about where the sentence ends, where the source's words begin, and who is speaking. The marks are the language's. Which glyphs enclose a quotation, which side of a closing mark a stop falls on, and how speech is conventionally set are stated in the resolved language's mechanics scope and not here, and the marks in the examples below stand in for whichever ones it names. What follows holds whatever they turn out to be — which setting a quotation is in, and what that setting then requires.

A run-in quotation is part of the sentence carrying it, and the joint between the two is punctuated by what the quoted words do there. Where the quotation is introduced as an utterance of its own, a stop stands at the joint and the quotation opens the way a sentence opens: *She replied, "I'll be there."* Where the quoted words are instead a grammatical part of the host sentence — its object, its complement, a fragment the sentence reads straight through — no stop stands at the joint and the quotation takes the case the surrounding syntax needs: *She called the proposal "completely unacceptable"*, not *She called the proposal, "Completely unacceptable"*. A stop at that joint promises the reader an utterance and then hands them a sentence with no room for one. Which of a comma and a colon introduces an utterance is a matter for the writer and for the language; whether a stop stands at the joint at all is neither.

The sentence around a run-in quotation still ends, and it ends once. A quoted sentence's own final stop and the host sentence's stop are one stop and not two, and where the quoted matter ends in a question or exclamation mark that mark stands alone and takes no comma beside it: *"Will you?" she asked*, not *"Will you?", she asked*. A reporting clause is bound to the utterance it reports rather than being a sentence in its own right, so it takes no capital and never stands behind a full stop: *"I'll come," she said*, not *"I'll come." She said.* Which side of the closing mark the surviving stop falls on is settled by the language and not here.

A block quotation is marked by being set off, and that setting is the whole of the mark. Marks enclosing a block state the quotation a second time, and they cost the reader the one thing the block was doing for them: inside a block, marks are the source's own and are preserved as the source wrote them. Because the block itself takes no level, a quotation inside one stands at the outermost level the language has rather than at the level it would take nested inside another.

The sentence introducing a block has finished by the time the block begins, and the block ends on the quoted matter's own punctuation, so the surrounding sentence's stop does not follow the block and no part of the host sentence is left hanging past it. A source named with a block sits outside the quotation and after it; set inside, the attribution reads as something the source wrote about itself.

Reported speech is punctuated as a run-in quotation is, and what the setting adds is the layout that says who is speaking. A turn belongs to one speaker and takes a paragraph of its own, and a second speaker beginning inside the first speaker's paragraph is read as the first speaker still talking, however plainly the words belong to somebody else. Where one speaker's turn runs across more than one paragraph, the continuation is marked as the same turn, because a reader shown nothing takes the second paragraph for somebody else's turn: a new paragraph is what a change of speaker looks like in this setting. How a language marks the continuation is its own — a turn left unclosed until its last paragraph, a speech mark opening every one of them — but that the reader can tell one continued turn from two is not the language's to settle.

A quotation promises that the words inside it are the source's, and three departures from that promise are each marked where they occur. Words added or altered so that the quotation fits its host sentence — a pronoun resolved, a tense harmonised, an initial capital raised or lowered to suit the surrounding syntax — are marked as the writer's rather than the source's: *"[T]he proposal was unacceptable"*. Words left out are marked at the gap, so that the reader is not shown a continuous sentence the source never wrote: *"the proposal … was unacceptable"*. An error the source made is kept and marked as the source's — *[sic]* — because quoted matter is not the text's own, and an error corrected inside a quotation makes the quotation false about its source. Unmarked, each of the three reads as the source's own words, which is the single thing the reader took the quotation to guarantee.

## Abbreviations spelled out

The capitals in an abbreviation are a property of the abbreviation and say nothing about the words behind it, so a spelled-out form is capitalised the way those same words are capitalised anywhere else in the text. *Search engine optimisation* and *hypertext markup language* are the forms; *Search Engine Optimisation* and *HyperText Markup Language* are the error, and it comes from reading the capitals backwards out of *SEO* and *HTML*. What it does to a reader is assert a name the text does not have: capitals in running prose mark a proper noun, and a reader meeting them takes the words for the title of a product, a standard, or an organisation rather than for a description of what the abbreviation stands for.

Where the words behind an abbreviation are a proper name, they keep the capitals the name has anyway: *North Atlantic Treaty Organization*, *World Health Organization*. That is the name's capitalisation and not the abbreviation's, which is why the abbreviation is no guide to it — *WHO* and *HTML* look alike, and the words behind them are not the same kind of thing. Correct at the spelled-out form and nowhere else: the abbreviation keeps its own capitals, and where and how the text introduces it is untouched.

## Lists

A list holds one convention for punctuation and capitalisation, and holds it in every item. Which convention it can hold follows from what the items are. Items that are complete sentences are punctuated as sentences, capital and terminal stop, because a sentence does not stop being one for sitting in a list; items that are fragments completing the sentence that introduces them are punctuated as parts of that sentence, and a list of fragments therefore has more than one correct treatment. What is wrong in either case is holding two at once, because the reader takes the change as meaning something: the fragment among sentences reads as truncated, and the one item ending in a stop reads as the end of the list.

Correct at the items that depart from the convention the rest of the list keeps, and nowhere else. The stop closing the last item of a list of fragments is the introducing sentence ending rather than a departure from the list's convention, and it stands. Where the items are genuinely of both kinds, what would have to change is an item and not its punctuation, and rewriting an item is past where a mechanical pass stops.

## Established variants

Where a language establishes more than one correct form, the text's own choice stands. A form is not an error because another form is more common, more modern, or the one the reader would have written, and the correction is never to normalise the text towards one of them. Only inconsistency within one text is corrected, and it is corrected towards whichever of the established forms that text already uses more.

That preserves nothing the rules in hand name as an error. A construction this contract or the resolved language's own mechanics guidance identifies as wrong is corrected however consistently the text commits to it, because consistency is what an established variant is judged by and never what makes something established. A text that is wrong the same way throughout is wrong throughout.
